set.name: Abracadabra AI glossary
set.description: Plain-English definitions of the AI, search and software terms used on abra-ca-dabra.app, each checked against primary sources.

terms.name: AI agent
terms.question: What is an AI agent?
terms.description: An AI agent is a program that uses an AI model to pick its own next step toward a goal, inside limits people set. Plain-English definition, sources and FAQs.
terms.short: An AI agent is a program that uses an AI model to choose its own next step toward a goal, such as checking a calendar or drafting a text. It works inside limits that people set.
explainer: The key word is choose. A normal program follows steps that someone wrote in advance. An agent looks at what it just found, then picks the next tool or action itself. Anthropic draws the line this way: in a workflow, the steps are set in code, and in an agent, the model directs its own process and its use of tools.

Google's glossary puts it in similar terms: software that can reason about what a person asks, then plan and carry out actions for them. In practice, the people who set it up still decide which tools it may use, what it may never send, and who can stop it.

sections.q: How is an AI agent different from a workflow?
a: A workflow repeats steps in an order you wrote down. An agent picks the order as it goes, based on what each step turns up. If you already know the steps, a workflow is often enough. Anthropic's own advice is to start with the simplest thing that works and add an agent only when the simple version falls short.

sections.q: Does an AI agent work without people?
a: It can act on its own between checkpoints, but it should not run without limits. Anthropic suggests clear stopping rules and points where the agent can pause for a person. On this site we keep a named person who can check the work and stop a send.

faqs.question: What is an AI agent in simple terms?
faqs.answer: An AI agent is a program that uses an AI model to decide its own next step toward a goal, such as looking up a booking or drafting a reply. People set the limits it works inside.

faqs.question: Is a chatbot an AI agent?
faqs.answer: Not always. A chatbot that only answers questions is not choosing actions. It becomes more like an agent when it can pick and use tools, such as a calendar or a search, to finish a task.

faqs.question: Do I need an AI agent or a workflow?
faqs.answer: If you can write the steps down in order and they rarely change, a workflow is usually enough. An agent fits work where the next step depends on what the last step found.

terms.changes: Added that an agent uses an AI model and works toward a goal inside limits people set. The draft alone would also fit a plain rule-based script.

terms.name: Generative engine optimization
terms.question: What is generative engine optimization?
terms.description: Generative engine optimization (GEO) means shaping pages so AI answer tools show and cite them. What it is, what Google says, and the research behind it.
terms.short: Generative engine optimization (GEO) is the work of shaping web pages so AI tools that write answers are more likely to show and cite them. Examples of these tools are Google's AI Overviews and Perplexity. Google says this work is still SEO.
explainer: The name comes from a research paper that called AI answer tools generative engines. These tools search the web, read a few pages, and write one answer with links to their sources. GEO asks how a page can earn a place in that answer.

Google's own guide says that, from its side, optimizing for these AI features is optimizing for search, so it is still SEO. A page must be indexed and allowed to show a snippet before Google's AI features can use it. The paper's authors tested changes such as adding sources, quotes and real numbers, and reported visibility gains of up to 40% in their test setup.

sections.q: Is GEO different from SEO?
a: Google says no, at least for Google Search. Its guide calls the AI features part of search and says the usual SEO advice still applies. Other AI tools may work in other ways, so the safe plan is one good page that serves both a list of links and a written answer.

sections.q: What does GEO work look like on a page?
a: It looks like good search work: a clear answer near the top, headings that match real questions, named sources, and facts a reader can check. Google lists files like llms.txt and splitting pages into small chunks as things you do not need for Google Search.

faqs.question: What does GEO stand for?
faqs.answer: GEO stands for generative engine optimization. It means shaping pages so AI tools that write answers are more likely to use and cite them.

faqs.question: Does Google treat GEO as separate from SEO?
faqs.answer: No. Google's guide says optimizing for its generative AI features is still SEO, and that the usual SEO best practices still apply.

faqs.question: Where did the term GEO come from?
faqs.answer: It was named in a research paper by Aggarwal and others, presented at the KDD conference. The paper measured how often a source shows up in answers written by AI search tools.

terms.name: Answer engine optimization
terms.question: What is answer engine optimization (AEO)?
terms.description: Answer engine optimization (AEO) is getting your pages used and cited in AI answers. A plain definition, how it relates to GEO, and what Google says.
terms.short: Answer engine optimization (AEO) is the work of getting your pages used and cited when an AI tool answers a question directly. Google says it is still SEO.
explainer: An answer engine replies with a written answer instead of only a list of links. AEO is the effort to be one of the sources that answer is built from, with a link back to your page.

Google's guide groups AEO with GEO. It says both terms describe work aimed at being seen in AI search, and that for Google this work is ordinary SEO. It also warns that many AEO and GEO "hacks" sold online do not match how Google Search works.

sections.q: How is AEO different from GEO?
a: In everyday use they mean almost the same thing. Google treats both as names for the same goal: being visible in AI search. We use AEO, GEO and SEO as one practice on this site.

sections.q: What helps a page get cited in an AI answer?
a: Google's advice is the same as for search: useful, original content, a clear structure, and a page Google can crawl and index with a snippet. A citation is not the same as a click, so it helps to measure both.

faqs.question: What does AEO stand for?
faqs.answer: AEO stands for answer engine optimization. It is the work of getting your pages used and cited when an AI tool writes an answer.

faqs.question: Is AEO the same as SEO?
faqs.answer: For Google Search, yes. Google says AEO and GEO are still SEO and that the usual best practices apply to its AI features.

faqs.question: Do I need a special file or markup for AEO?
faqs.answer: Not for Google. Google says you do not need new AI text files, special markup or chopped up pages to appear in its AI features.

terms.name: Large language model
terms.question: What is a large language model (LLM)?
terms.description: A large language model (LLM) is an AI model trained on huge amounts of text that writes by predicting the next word. Plain definition, examples and limits.
terms.short: A large language model (LLM) is an AI model trained on a huge amount of text. It writes by predicting the next word, or part of a word, over and over. Google's Gemini and OpenAI's GPT models are examples.
explainer: Google's course describes an LLM as a model that predicts a token or a run of tokens, where a token can be a word, part of a word, or a single character. Strung together, those guesses become sentences and whole answers. That is why an LLM can draft a reply, sum up a page or answer a question in plain language.

Most chat tools you have heard of run on an LLM. The model does not look facts up by itself. Google's course notes that LLMs can make up wrong answers, which is why tools that cite their sources, and a person who checks the work, matter.

sections.q: How does a large language model write?
a: It predicts what comes next, one small piece at a time. Google's course calls LLMs autocomplete that can predict thousands of tokens in a row. Training on a huge amount of text teaches it which words tend to follow which.

sections.q: Can a large language model be wrong?
a: Yes. Google lists made up answers, high computing cost and bias among the known problems with LLMs. Grounding the model in real sources and having a person review the output lowers the risk.

faqs.question: What does LLM stand for?
faqs.answer: LLM stands for large language model. It is an AI model trained on a huge amount of text so it can read and write language.

faqs.question: Is ChatGPT a large language model?
faqs.answer: ChatGPT is a chat product built on OpenAI's GPT models, and those models are large language models. Google's glossary names GPT and Gemini as examples.

faqs.question: Why do large language models make mistakes?
faqs.answer: An LLM writes by predicting likely words, not by checking facts. Google's course says LLMs can hallucinate, which means their answers can contain mistakes.

refs.title: LLMs: What's a large language model?

terms.name: llms.txt
terms.question: What is llms.txt?
terms.description: llms.txt is a proposed Markdown file that gives AI tools a site summary and key links. What goes in it, where it lives, and why Google Search ignores it.
terms.short: llms.txt is a proposed file, written in Markdown, that gives AI tools a short summary of a website and links to its most useful pages. It usually sits at the site's root, at /llms.txt. Google Search says it does not use the file.
explainer: Jeremy Howard published the proposal at llmstxt.org and updated it in August 2026. The file starts with the site's name and a one line summary, then lists links with short notes. AI tools are meant to read it when they need to learn about a site, then follow only the links they need.

The newest version says the file can sit at the root or under a path, such as a docs folder, to cover just that part of the site. Google's guide says Google Search ignores llms.txt, so it neither helps nor hurts your Google rankings. Other tools may still read it.

sections.q: Does Google use llms.txt?
a: No. Google says you do not need AI text files like llms.txt to appear in Google Search or its AI features, because Google Search does not use them. It also says it is fine to keep one for other services that do.

sections.q: What goes in an llms.txt file?
a: The proposal asks for a title line, a short summary, and then lists of links, each with an optional note. An Optional section can hold links a tool may skip. This site has its own file at /llms.txt.

faqs.question: What is llms.txt used for?
faqs.answer: It gives AI tools a short, clean guide to a website: a summary plus links to the pages that matter most, so a tool can find what it needs without reading every page.

faqs.question: Does llms.txt help my Google ranking?
faqs.answer: No. Google says Google Search ignores llms.txt, so the file will neither help nor harm your visibility or rankings in Google.

faqs.question: Is llms.txt the same as robots.txt?
faqs.answer: No. robots.txt tells crawlers which pages they may visit. llms.txt is a guide that points AI tools to useful pages when they need information.

terms.name: AI readiness
terms.question: What is AI readiness?
terms.description: AI readiness is how prepared a business is to put an AI tool to work: its data, processes, people and decisions. A plain definition and how to check it.
terms.short: AI readiness is how prepared a business is to put an AI tool to work and get value from it. It depends on the business more than the tool. That means its data, the way work gets done, its people and who makes decisions.
explainer: A business can buy a strong tool and still get little from it. AWS makes the same point in its checklist for smaller firms: readiness is not just a technology choice. It covers your information, your workflows, your people and the rules for how AI is used and checked.

On this site we score readiness in four parts: data, process, people and the decision. The goal is to find the one weak spot to fix first, before anyone pays for a tool. Our Readiness Check is one way to see where you stand.

sections.q: What makes a business ready for AI?
a: The facts a job needs are in one place a system can read, the steps are written down, someone has time to check the output, and one person owns the decision. AWS's checklist names the same areas: data, workflows, people and governance.

sections.q: How do you measure AI readiness?
a: With an assessment that scores each area, so the gap is plain. AWS describes an AI readiness assessment as a structured look at data, technology, processes and people. Our Readiness Check gives a band and a few next steps.

faqs.question: What is AI readiness in simple terms?
faqs.answer: AI readiness is how prepared a business is to use an AI tool well. It depends on its data, its processes, its people and who owns the decision, more than on the tool itself.

faqs.question: Why does AI readiness matter before buying a tool?
faqs.answer: A tool cannot fix scattered data or steps nobody wrote down. Checking readiness first shows what to fix so the tool has a real job to do.

faqs.question: How can I check my AI readiness?
faqs.answer: Use an assessment that scores data, process, people and decisions. The Abracadabra Readiness Check takes five to seven minutes and gives you a band and suggestions.

terms.name: Machine learning
terms.question: What is machine learning?
terms.description: Machine learning is software that learns patterns from past data and predicts on new data. A plain-English definition with Google's wording and examples.
terms.short: Machine learning is a way to build software that learns patterns from past data. It does not rely only on rules a person wrote. The trained model can then make predictions about new data, such as next month's orders.
explainer: Google's glossary defines it as a program or system that trains a model from input data, so the model can make useful predictions from new data. It works best when the new data looks like the data it learned from. If the past is a poor guide to the future, the predictions will be poor too.

Machine learning is a broad field. Large language models are one kind of machine learning model, built for text. Many business uses are smaller and plainer: a forecast of demand, a flag on a record that looks off, or an estimate with a range around it.

sections.q: How does machine learning work?
a: You give it many past examples, and training adjusts a model until its guesses match those examples well. Then you use the trained model on new cases. Testing it on data it has not seen tells you if it really learned the pattern.

sections.q: When is machine learning worth it for a business?
a: When you have enough history to learn from and a question you ask often, such as how much stock to order. If simple rules already do the job, keep the rules. We only switch to a learned model when it beats them in testing.

faqs.question: What is machine learning in simple terms?
faqs.answer: Machine learning is software that learns patterns from past data, then uses what it learned to make predictions about new data.

faqs.question: Is machine learning the same as AI?
faqs.answer: Machine learning is one part of AI. It covers systems that learn from data, including the large language models behind many chat tools.

faqs.question: How much data does machine learning need?
faqs.answer: There is no single number. It needs enough past examples that look like the cases you will predict, and you test it on data it has not seen to check it learned.

terms.name: Gradient boosting
terms.question: What is gradient boosting?
terms.description: Gradient boosting builds one strong model from many small decision trees, each one learning from the errors left. A plain definition, sourced to Google.
terms.short: Gradient boosting is a machine learning method that builds one strong model out of many weak ones. The weak ones are usually small decision trees. Each new tree learns from the errors the model still makes. It is added in a small step to shrink them.
explainer: Google's course explains it with two kinds of model: a weak one, typically a small decision tree, and a strong one made of many weak ones added together. At each step a new weak model is trained to predict the current error, then added to the strong model to reduce it. When the weak models are decision trees, the result is called gradient boosted trees.

A setting called shrinkage scales each new tree down before it is added. Google compares it to a learning rate: smaller steps learn more slowly but help stop the model from fitting noise. Training stops at a set limit, or when results on held back data stop improving.

sections.q: Why use gradient boosting?
a: Google's course says decision forests, the family gradient boosted trees belong to, work well on table data, such as rows of past orders with a number to predict. Each new tree only has to fix what the model before it got wrong, so the model improves step by step.

sections.q: Can gradient boosting overfit?
a: Yes. Google notes that the strong model can begin to overfit, meaning it fits the training data too closely. Shrinkage and stopping when results on a separate check set get worse help prevent that.

faqs.question: What is gradient boosting in simple terms?
faqs.answer: Gradient boosting builds a model from many small decision trees, one after another. Each new tree learns from the mistakes the model still makes.

faqs.question: What are gradient boosted trees?
faqs.answer: Gradient boosted trees are gradient boosting with decision trees as the weak models. Google's course uses this name for the most common form of the method.

faqs.question: Is gradient boosting a kind of machine learning?
faqs.answer: Yes. It is a machine learning method that combines many weak models, usually small decision trees, into one stronger model.

terms.name: Schema markup and JSON-LD
terms.question: What are schema markup and JSON-LD?
terms.description: Schema markup labels what a page is about using schema.org; JSON-LD is the format Google recommends for it. Plain definitions, sources and FAQs.
terms.short: Schema markup is code added to a web page that labels what the page is about, such as an article, a product or a business. The labels come from a shared list called schema.org. JSON-LD is the format Google recommends for it. It is a block of code that machines read and visitors do not see.
explainer: Google calls this structured data: a standard way to give clear clues about a page and sort its content. Most of it uses the schema.org vocabulary, which names types like Organization, Product and FAQPage and the facts each can carry.

JSON-LD is a W3C standard for writing linked data as JSON. On a web page it sits in its own script block, apart from the text people read, which is why Google calls it the easiest format to set up and maintain. The rule that matters most: the markup must describe what is really on the page.

sections.q: Does schema markup help with AI search?
a: Google says structured data is not required for its generative AI features, and there is no special markup for them. It still recommends structured data as part of normal SEO, because it can make a page eligible for rich results.

sections.q: What is the difference between schema markup and JSON-LD?
a: Schema markup is what you say about the page, using schema.org types and properties. JSON-LD is one way to write it down. Microdata and RDFa are the other two formats Google supports.

faqs.question: What is schema markup in simple terms?
faqs.answer: Schema markup is code that tells search engines what a page is about. It might label an article, a product or a set of questions. The labels come from schema.org.

faqs.question: Why does Google recommend JSON-LD?
faqs.answer: Google says JSON-LD is the easiest format for site owners to set up and keep up at scale. It sits in its own block, so it is not mixed into the text people read.

faqs.question: Can schema markup include things not shown on the page?
faqs.answer: It should not. Google says not to add structured data about information that visitors cannot see, even if it is accurate.

terms.name: Agentic AI
terms.question: What is agentic AI?
terms.description: Agentic AI is a broad label for AI that works toward a goal with limited supervision, often through AI agents. How it differs from an AI agent.
terms.short: Agentic AI is a broad label for AI systems that can work toward a goal with limited supervision. It usually means one or more AI agents that plan steps and use tools. Sometimes several agents work together.
explainer: IBM defines agentic AI as a system that can reach a specific goal with limited supervision, made up of AI agents. In a system with many agents, each one handles part of the job and the work is coordinated. Google's glossary says agentic simply refers to the qualities agents have, such as autonomy.

The label is used loosely. Anthropic uses agentic systems to cover both fixed workflows and true agents. Vendors often use agentic AI for a large program of many agents. On this site we use the plainer phrase AI that takes actions on its own, and we ask which single job it does and who can stop it.

sections.q: What is the difference between AI agents and agentic AI?
a: An AI agent is one system that picks its own next step. Agentic AI is the wider label for AI that acts with limited supervision, which can mean one agent or many working together. Buy for the job, not the label.

sections.q: Is agentic AI the same as generative AI?
a: No. IBM explains that generative AI makes content, such as text or images, while agentic AI uses that output to reach a goal, for example by calling outside tools to finish a task.

faqs.question: What does agentic AI mean?
faqs.answer: Agentic AI means AI systems that can work toward a goal with limited supervision, usually through one or more AI agents that plan steps and use tools.

faqs.question: Is agentic AI the same as an AI agent?
faqs.answer: Not quite. An AI agent is a single system. Agentic AI is the broader label for AI that acts on its own, often built from several agents.

faqs.question: Does agentic AI need human oversight?
faqs.answer: Yes. Its ability to act on its own is the point and the risk. Clear goals, limits and a person who can review or stop the work keep it on track.
